content: Active screening and ensuring 100% treatment completion in targeted areas are critical components of leprosy control programs. In the first year of implementation, awareness campaigns followed by active case finding were conducted across eight provinces, leading to the identification of 1,488 new leprosy cases. These cases were promptly provided with multidrug therapy (MDT). This represents a 75% increase in case detection compared to the previous year. Soon, treatment outcomes for patients with paucibacillary (PB) leprosy will be available to assess improvements in case management quality. In 2016, the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) planned to expand active screening activities to additional geographical areas as part of a multi-year project. This includes investigations and screening of families and communities in response to leprosy detection in children, whether or not they present with Grade 2 Disabilities (G2D). Silent communities, which are geographically close to endemic areas or have similar social and infrastructure conditions, or those with previously reported leprosy cases, are also targeted for screening. To ensure effective leprosy management, trained healthcare workers must be available at regional and central levels, with an adequate number of female staff and proper facilities for patient examination and classification. Leprosy should be integrated into the curricula of clinical nurses and medical doctors, including specialized fields like dermatology. Countries with high endemicity or high G2D rates due to weak health systems must address these challenges. Silent zones, where leprosy cases are no longer reported, require investigation to determine whether transmission has truly ceased or if detection and reporting systems are inadequate. Each country must map its leprosy situation and plan interventions accordingly. In Cambodia, the leprosy program, in collaboration with the Novartis Foundation and CIOMAL, conducted contact surveys in 2015 in high-burden areas. These surveys covered household and neighbor contacts within a 300-meter radius of index cases registered in the past 10 years. Community health workers identified suspects, who were later confirmed by healthcare workers in health facilities. This approach has consistently increased case detection rates, aiming for earlier detection and reduced transmission among high-risk groups and in high-burden areas. Egypt achieved the WHO leprosy elimination target at the national level in 1994 and at the governorate and district levels in 2004. However, 18 villages in six governorates, primarily in the southern part of the country, have not yet reached this goal. Approximately 60% of new leprosy cases in Egypt originate from these six governorates, with the majority from the 18 villages. The Ministry of Health and Population is intensifying efforts in these hotspots to consolidate achievements and accelerate progress toward a leprosy-free country. Activities include strengthening the capacity of healthcare workers in primary health clinics, implementing active screening among residents of the 18 villages, increasing community awareness to encourage self-reporting, and engaging community leaders to reduce stigma and promote patient rehabilitation. In Paraguay, the Mennonite Hospital Km 81, located in a rural area 81 kilometers from the capital Asunción, serves as a referral center for leprosy treatment and training for medical and nursing students. Through an agreement with a prominent nursing school, all third-year students are required to participate in practical lessons at this hospital for two days, focusing on leprosy and tuberculosis. They then conduct health education sessions in high schools and perform house-to-house active screening for skin patches and prolonged cough. This initiative, started in 2009, has increased case detection and raised awareness about leprosy at minimal financial cost. Multidrug therapy (MDT) is a highly effective and safe treatment for leprosy, preventing the emergence of drug resistance. Leprosy should never be treated with a single drug. MDT is provided free of charge to all patients through donations from Novartis, coordinated globally by the World Health Organization (WHO). National ministries of health manage the distribution to ensure no shortages at health facilities, enabling prompt treatment initiation to halt disease transmission. Irregular treatment or drug shortages can lead to non-adherence and resistance. MDT is safe during pregnancy, breastfeeding, and for HIV-positive patients, including those on antiretroviral or tuberculosis treatment. The standard adult MDT regimen for multibacillary (MB) leprosy includes rifampicin (600 mg once monthly), clofazimine (300 mg once monthly and 50 mg daily), and dapsone (100 mg daily) for 12 months. For PB leprosy, the regimen includes rifampicin (600 mg once monthly) and dapsone (100 mg daily) for six months. Pediatric regimens are adjusted based on weight and age. MDT blister packs, containing four weeks of treatment, are convenient and ensure proper dosing. Efforts must be made to ensure treatment compliance, with PB cases completing six months of treatment within nine months and MB cases completing 12 months within 18 months. Rarely, treatment may be extended based on clinical and bacteriological evidence. Studies suggest the possibility of shortening MB treatment to six months, potentially introducing a uniform MDT regimen for both PB and MB cases. WHO will issue new guidelines once sufficient evidence supports this change. MDT is generally safe, with serious adverse effects being rare. Minor side effects, such as red urine (rifampicin) or skin discoloration (clofazimine), can be managed with reassurance or counseling. Severe reactions, such as jaundice or renal failure, require stopping the drug and referral to specialized centers. Alternative regimens should only be used in cases of severe intolerance or resistance. Programs must ensure treatment adherence and evaluate performance based on treatment completion rates, a core programmatic indicator. Resources for tracing patients who abandon treatment, such as mobile phones and home visits, should be available. A patient-centered approach is essential to facilitate adherence. Annual refresher training on recording and reporting leprosy cases is necessary to ensure accurate cohort analysis of treatment completion. Research on adherence and its improvement should be encouraged. Periodic supervision and monitoring, including patient interviews, are crucial to ensure regular and free treatment provision.
